# Claims adjudication

35 claims circulating in marketing, journalism and clinical
conversation, each checked against the evidence rows.

| Verdict | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Supported | 3 |
| Partially supported | 8 |
| Misleading | 7 |
| Unsupported | 12 |
| False | 5 |

## Supported

| ID | Claim | What the evidence shows | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL-04 | Fish oil lowers triglycerides by 20-30% | At 4 g/day, prescription-grade EPA+DHA or EPA alone lowers triglycerides 20-30% in hypertriglyceridaemia; at 1 g/day the effect is much smaller. The claim is true only at pharmacological doses. | LIP-01 |
| CL-28 | DHA is essential for infant brain development | DHA is structurally required in retinal and neural membranes, and breast-milk DHA responds to maternal intake. What is not supported is the claim that supplementing already well-nourished mothers or children raises IQ. | PRG-05 |
| CL-33 | Omega-3 reduces inflammation | CRP falls by about 0.4 SMD across meta-analyses, but the effect is attenuated in obesity and has not translated into reliable clinical benefit in most diseases. | OTH-03 |

## Partially supported

| ID | Claim | What the evidence shows | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL-01 | Fish oil prevents heart attacks in healthy people | In VITAL, 1 g/day reduced total myocardial infarction by 28% (HR 0.72) but did not reduce the primary composite of MI, stroke and cardiovascular death. A 28% MI reduction in one large trial is a real signal, not a licence to claim general prevention. | CV-01, CV-02 |
| CL-06 | Omega-3 lowers blood pressure | Pooled trials show about -2.6/-1.6 mmHg at 2-3 g/day, and about -4.5 mmHg systolic in hypertensive adults. Real but modest, and not a substitute for antihypertensive treatment. | CV-15 |
| CL-10 | EPA is the antidepressant component of fish oil | Meta-regression and dose-subgroup analyses consistently favour EPA-predominant formulations, but the trials are small and heterogeneous. This is a hypothesis with weak support, not an established mechanism. | MEN-01, MEN-02 |
| CL-18 | Fish oil supplements are free of mercury | Refined body oils are consistently low in mercury in market surveys, and EU law caps supplements at 0.10 mg/kg. Shark and cod liver oils are recurring outliers for other persistent pollutants, so 'free of mercury' is not the same as 'free of contaminants'. |  |
| CL-19 | If a capsule smells fishy it is rancid | Fishy odour indicates volatile oxidation products and is a reasonable warning sign, but odour is a poor quantitative marker and flavoured oils confound sensory judgement. Only peroxide value, p-anisidine value and TOTOX measure it. |  |
| CL-27 | Omega-3 prevents preterm birth | Cochrane's pooled analysis shows a large reduction in early preterm birth (RR 0.58), but the largest single trial (ORIP, 5,544 women) was null. Benefit may depend on baseline DHA status and dose. Prenatal use should be a clinical decision. | PRG-01, PRG-03 |
| CL-30 | Fish oil supplements are a sustainable source of omega-3 | Fish oil is largely a by-product of a fishery that is 64% directed to aquaculture feed, and Peruvian anchoveta supply is climate-sensitive. Algal oil and certified by-product oils reduce pressure on wild stocks; MSC/FOS logos certify sourcing, not potency. |  |
| CL-32 | Fish oil helps joint pain | Small trials show a modest effect (SMD about -0.3), but the largest and best-controlled trials - VITAL's knee substudy and a 2024 krill-oil MRI trial - were null. At best a minor adjunct. | MSK-01, MSK-02, MSK-03 |

## Misleading

| ID | Claim | What the evidence shows | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL-03 | Four grams of fish oil cuts heart attack risk by 25% | The 25% figure comes from REDUCE-IT, which used 4 g/day of icosapent ethyl - a purified EPA-only ethyl ester drug - not ordinary fish oil, and used a mineral-oil placebo whose effect on the result is contested. STRENGTH, testing 4 g/day EPA+DHA, found no benefit (HR 0.99). | CV-10, CV-11 |
| CL-15 | Cod liver oil is a risk-free way to get omega-3 | Cod liver oil carries preformed vitamin A. Carlson's product supplies 255 mcg RAE per teaspoon (8.5% of the adult upper limit), but typical cod liver oils supply about 1,350 mcg RAE per teaspoon (45% of the UL), and high-vitamin products can exceed it. Cod liver oil is a vitamin supplement as much as an omega-3 one. |  |
| CL-17 | Re-esterified triglyceride is 70% more bioavailable than fish oil | In the most-cited trial, rTG achieved 124% of natural fish oil's relative bioavailability (134% dose-adjusted) - a real but modest advantage, measured over two weeks in 72 people, not a 70% advantage over every product. |  |
| CL-21 | IFOS 5-star certification means pharmaceutical grade | IFOS tests lots for potency, contaminants and oxidation and publishes results. That is valuable, but 'pharmaceutical grade' is a marketing term with no legal definition, and lot certification does not make a supplement a drug. |  |
| CL-22 | USP Verified means the supplement works | USP verification covers identity, potency, contaminants, dissolution and GMP - quality attributes, not clinical efficacy. A verified product can still be clinically useless. |  |
| CL-25 | High-dose fish oil is dangerous for the heart | High-dose omega-3 raises atrial fibrillation risk dose-dependently (HR 1.25 overall; 1.49 above 1 g/day; 1.69 at 3 g/day in STRENGTH). That is a real safety signal, but it is not the same as causing heart attacks. | CV-12, CV-13 |
| CL-31 | Molecularly distilled means contaminant-free | Distillation removes most dioxins and PCBs (76-99% in published studies) but does not reverse oxidation already present, and the process can strip vitamins. 'Distilled' is a process claim, not a test result. |  |

## Unsupported

| ID | Claim | What the evidence shows | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL-02 | Omega-3 supplements reduce the risk of dying from any cause | Cochrane's high-certainty pooled estimate is RR 0.97 (0.93-1.01) across 45 trials and 143,693 participants. No mortality benefit is demonstrable. | CV-05 |
| CL-05 | Omega-3 raises HDL cholesterol | Effects on HDL are small and inconsistent, and not a basis for supplementation. Triglyceride lowering is the reproducible lipid effect. | LIP-01, LIP-03 |
| CL-07 | Omega-3 prevents dementia | Every adequately powered RCT of supplements is null for incident dementia and cognitive decline (RR 0.98). Observational fish-intake associations are likely confounded. | NEU-02, NEU-03 |
| CL-08 | Omega-3 improves memory in healthy adults | Cochrane found no effect on MMSE or any cognitive domain in healthy older adults; the largest meta-analysis found an MMSE difference of 0.10 points, which is clinically meaningless. | NEU-01, NEU-02 |
| CL-09 | Fish oil cures depression | The pooled effect in major depression is small (SMD about 0.4) with high heterogeneity, and the evidence is low certainty. It is at most an adjunct, never a treatment. | MEN-01 |
| CL-11 | Omega-3 helps children with ADHD | Cochrane's 2023 review of 37 RCTs found high-certainty no effect on parent-rated ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.08). | MEN-07 |
| CL-13 | Krill oil is better absorbed so you need less | Equal-dose comparisons have not shown superior absorption; a network meta-analysis found no difference in triglyceride lowering between krill and fish oil per gram of EPA+DHA. Krill works because it contains omega-3, not because it is magic. |  |
| CL-23 | Omega-3 thins the blood dangerously | Meta-analysis of 120,643 patients found bleeding RR 1.09 (0.91-1.31). A small absolute increase appears with high-dose purified EPA. The risk is not zero but is far smaller than the marketing counter-claim implies. | SAF-01 |
| CL-24 | Stop fish oil seven days before surgery | The OPERA trial gave 8-10 g/day of EPA+DHA before cardiac surgery and found no increase in major bleeding (OR 0.81) and fewer transfusions. No major guideline mandates a stop interval. | SAF-04 |
| CL-26 | Fish oil is good for dry eyes | DREAM, the largest trial (3 g/day, 535 patients), was null, and Cochrane found no clinically meaningful symptom benefit. | EYE-01, EYE-02 |
| CL-29 | Omega-3 builds muscle | Effects on muscle mass are small (about +0.33 kg) and disappear when one cancer trial is excluded; muscle protein synthesis is unchanged, and the largest 3-year trial was null. | MSK-06, MSK-07 |
| CL-35 | Omega-3 prevents cancer | VITAL found no reduction in invasive cancer (HR 1.03), and cohort analyses of colorectal cancer are null (RR 0.98). | CAN-01, CAN-02 |

## False

| ID | Claim | What the evidence shows | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL-12 | Krill oil is 50 times more potent than fish oil | Krill oil is roughly 12-19% EPA+DHA by mass - lower concentration than concentrated fish oil. Per-gram potency claims rely on conflating phospholipid content or astaxanthin with EPA+DHA. |  |
| CL-14 | Algae oil is inferior to fish oil | Algal DHA is bioequivalent to fish-derived DHA in controlled trials, and algal EPA+DHA lowered triglycerides comparably to fish oil at matched doses. Algal oils are the only vegan source with direct EPA+DHA evidence. |  |
| CL-16 | Ethyl ester fish oil is absorbed as well as triglyceride fish oil | Ethyl esters are absorbed at roughly 20% of the free-fatty-acid reference when taken without a fatty meal, and about 73% relative bioavailability versus natural triglyceride in the best-controlled comparison. Absorption improves substantially with a fat-containing meal. |  |
| CL-20 | TOTOX above 26 is illegal in the United States | There is no US regulatory limit for oxidation in fish oil supplements. TOTOX 26 is a voluntary GOED/Codex standard that some products exceed. |  |
| CL-34 | More EPA is always better | Triglyceride lowering saturates and atrial fibrillation risk rises with dose. Above 2-3 g/day, benefit must be weighed against AF risk; above 5 g/day the FDA has said the evidence is insufficient for its safety claim. | CV-12, CV-15 |
